25.0.0.en: Festus took over the governorship of Palestine, whose seat was Caesarea. He remained in the governorship two years, and was a just man. Because Jerusalem is the largest city of his province, he went up to it three days after taking over the governorship in Caesarea.

25.1.0.en: The chief of the Jews: the members of their highest council, that is, the Sanhedrin.

25.1.1.en: Desired favour against him: asking that he grant them a favor and be gracious to them by accepting their complaint and renewing the trial of Paul.

25.1.2.en: In Jerusalem, the Jews renewed their complaint to Festus against Paul through their high priest and the members of the Sanhedrin, and asked him to do them a service by bringing Paul to Jerusalem to try him there. Sadly, they had secretly plotted to kill him on the road from Caesarea to Jerusalem, as they had plotted before.

25.2.0.en: Festus did not agree, because he was about to go to Caesarea quickly, and he commanded that Paul be kept in Caesarea. This was by God's arrangement to protect Paul.

25.3.0.en: Festus asked the Jews to send down with him a delegation representing them to bring the case in Caesarea.

25.4.0.en: Festus stayed ten days in Jerusalem, then came to Caesarea and began to try Paul the day after his return. This shows his activity and his justice.

25.5.0.en: They brought Paul, and the Jews began to make many complaints against him with religious and civil charges, grave and false, which they were not able to prove.

25.6.0.en: Paul's defense centered on the fact that he was innocent of any charge against the Law, or the temple, or Caesar. These are the same three accusations that had been directed against him two years earlier before Felix the governor (ch. 24:5-6).

25.7.0.en: To do the Jews a pleasure: to be gracious to them and appease them and give them a gift, which was the trial of Paul in Jerusalem as they requested.

25.7.1.en: Because of the pressure of the Jews on Festus to resume the trial in Jerusalem, he tried to appease them. On the other hand, since he saw Paul's innocence, he asked him whether he wished to be tried in Jerusalem so as to obtain a civil and religious acquittal. Here the justice of Festus appears in two matters:

25.7.2.en: 1- That the religious trial in Jerusalem would take place in the presence of Festus, to keep him safe from any injustice.

25.7.3.en: 2- That he asked him whether he wished to go to Jerusalem or not.

25.8.0.en: Since Paul knew the cunning and tricks of the Jews, he protested that he was in the official court of the capital of Palestine at Caesarea, and that he was innocent, as the governor knew. In this he used his civil right as a Roman to nullify the deceit and evil of the Jews, especially since he was innocent by the testimony of the governor himself after his trials before him.

25.9.0.en: Paul declared that he was not asking for his acquittal as a gift from anyone, but that he was in fact innocent. How then could the governor hand him over to their counsel to kill him? He also declared his appeal of the case to the court of Caesar in Rome. This was his right as a Roman in such circumstances.

25.10.0.en: Festus suspended the hearing of the case as a formal procedure, and consulted his counselors, who recommended accepting Paul's request because it was lawful. So Festus declared to Paul that his appeal was accepted, and that he would go to the court of Caesar in Rome as he had requested.

25.10.1.en: St. Paul did not lose an opportunity to spread the ministry, even in Rome the capital. His personal case did not occupy his thought, but how he might go to Rome to preach in it. This is the true servant who counts nothing until he fulfills his ministry (ch. 20:24). Seize every opportunity to show Christ through your words and actions, and offer love to everyone you meet, and thus you show Christ to all.

25.11.s.en: (2) The meeting of Festus and Agrippa

25.11.0.en: Agrippa: a ruler over regions next to Judea, the son of the Herod whom the angel of the Lord smote with worms and who died in A.D. 44 after he had killed the Apostle James the Great. Agrippa was king over some regions adjoining Judea, and he showed his interest in the Jewish religion, but he betrayed the Jews at the destruction of Jerusalem.

25.11.1.en: Bernice: Agrippa's sister, who lived with him in adultery after her widowhood.

25.11.2.en: Agrippa and his sister Bernice came to greet Festus and congratulate him on the new governorship.

25.12.0.en: Their visit was prolonged, so Festus laid before them the matter of Paul, who had been in custody since the days of the previous governor Felix.

25.13.0.en: The chief of the Jews and their priests tried to obtain a sentence of condemnation against him.

25.14.0.en: Festus adhered to Roman law, which forbids a death sentence without trial and defense.

25.15.0.en: When the Jews came to Caesarea and Festus tried him face to face with them, they were not able to prove their accusations, and Festus found no crime in him against Roman law.

25.16.0.en: Festus informed Agrippa that the disputes between the Jews and Paul were religious, and they differed about a person called Jesus, whom the Jews said was dead, but Paul said was alive.

25.17.0.en: Because of this Festus was hesitant whether to release him or not. For he was innocent civilly, and so he asked him whether he wished to be tried religiously in the synagogue council of Jerusalem to obtain religious acquittal also.

25.18.0.en: Paul refused to go to Jerusalem, and appealed his case to Caesar, who was entitled "Augustus," that is, the one revered with the reverence due to gods. Thus it became necessary to send him to Caesar.

25.19.0.en: Agrippa asked to hear Paul out of his longing to hear more about Christianity, and Festus promised him that he would let him hear him the next day.

25.19.1.en: Perhaps God wished to give Agrippa and his sister the opportunity of hearing the preaching and repentance so that they might repent. For God seeks the repentance of all His children, whatever their conduct, but how many important opportunities like this one a person loses!

25.19.2.en: So know that every spiritual word or guidance you hear in the Church or outside it is a personal message for you to apply in your life, and not a general sermon concerning others.

25.20.0.en: Chief captains: they are the commanders of thousands of Roman soldiers.

25.20.1.en: Festus held a great celebration for Agrippa, who came with Bernice, and at the celebration were the chief commanders of the army with the great men of the city, then they brought Paul to the hall of audience.

25.21.0.en: Festus opened the session by presenting Paul, whom the Jews had sought by every means to kill in Jerusalem and Caesarea.

25.22.0.en: Although he had found nothing in his deeds deserving death, yet because Paul had appealed to Caesar, Festus agreed to send him to him.

25.23.0.en: Festus had found no specific charge to write in the letter referring the case to Caesar, whom he called "my lord," and perhaps this session would help him determine the charges, especially since King Agrippa knows Judaism well, so Festus would find what to write.

25.24.0.en: Festus made clear that it is folly to refer a case to the emperor without a reason, otherwise this would show his incompetence as a governor in examining cases.

25.24.1.en: God was still alerting Festus to faith through the words and case of Paul, whose innocence appears clearly. For God seeks the salvation of all.

25.24.2.en: Thus this council is the fifth defense since the arrest of Paul in Jerusalem: the first was before the crowds of the Jews in the temple, the second before the council of the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, the third before Felix in Caesarea, the fourth before Festus in Caesarea, and the fifth, this one, before King Agrippa and Festus in Caesarea. And through all this Paul was innocent by the testimony of those who tried him.

25.24.3.en: We must not be surprised if the showing of our innocence is delayed. For to everything under heaven there is a time, and we are not greater or more righteous than the great Apostle Paul. So accept being accused falsely, and if you defend yourself and they do not hear you, do not be disturbed, knowing that your endurance is very precious in God's sight and He rewards you for it, and He is able at the right time to show your innocence.

26.0.0.en: Agrippa, as president of the celebration, permitted Paul to begin presenting his point of view.

26.0.1.en: So Paul stretched forth his hand, bound with the chain, and began by saying that he was happy to be tried before a king who knows Judaism and is able to understand his religious point of view.

26.1.0.en: Paul made clear that King Agrippa knows the details of the Jewish religion, so that some supposed that he had become a Jew; therefore he would explain to him in some detail, because the Roman governors do not care about matters of Jewish worship.

26.2.0.en: The most straitest sect of our religion: the Pharisees were famous for the literal exactness of the Law and the setting down of many rules for that, with neglect of the spiritual meaning, so worship was emptied of its depth and became a constraint on people in their conduct.

26.2.1.en: Paul made clear that he grew up a Jew, and was brought up in Jerusalem to study the Law and was well known for that, and that he lived as a follower of the sect of the Pharisees, strict in the rites and the keeping of the commandments.

26.3.0.en: The hope of the promise: of the expected Messiah who will save His people and redeem them by His death and then His resurrection.

26.3.1.en: Our twelve tribes: all the Jews.

26.3.2.en: Paul declared his faith in eternal life and the resurrection from the dead, which was accomplished in Christ the expected Messiah. He linked the faith of the Jews in the Messiah with the resurrection of this Messiah from the dead, so he believes in the Messiah like the Jews, and this faith of theirs is the aim of their continual worship night and day, and consequently there is no need to try him, because he agrees with them in faith in the Messiah.

26.4.0.en: Paul asks why it should be hard for a Jew to believe the resurrection of the dead in general and of Christ in particular. Did not the Old Testament mention several times the raising of the dead by Elijah and Elisha?

26.5.0.en: Paul mentions that when he was a Jew, he was determined to oppose Christ and Christianity, because he supposed it to be foreign to Judaism and did not understand that it is its completion.

26.6.0.en: Paul acknowledged his persecution of the Christians in Jerusalem as all the Jews know, using the authority of the chief priests to imprison and kill many of the Jews who had become Christians, since he was a member of the Sanhedrin, and at the end of the trial of each, the members cast lots to make sure of his condemnation or innocence before killing him, and Paul took part in that also, and the casting of votes was done mostly by voting and the majority of opinions.

26.7.0.en: Paul's activity extended to the synagogues of Jerusalem, Judea and elsewhere, so he sentenced the Christians to beating and scourging until they would deny the name of Christ, and he was furious against them and drove them out beyond the province of Judea.

26.7.1.en: Paul wronged Christ supposing that this was the truth. So do not rush in your actions, but review yourself and listen to the counsel of guides lest you wrong the innocent or declare mistaken opinions.

26.8.s.en: (2) The vision and the change of life

26.8.0.en: Paul acknowledges that on one occasion he was going to Damascus with letters and commissions from the chief priests to seize the Christians and kill them.

26.9.0.en: Here Paul tells for the third time of Christ's meeting with him on the way to Damascus (ch. 9:3, 22:6). On the way at noon, he saw a light from heaven, above the brightness of the noonday sun, shining round about him and those with him, as happened at the Transfiguration.

26.10.0.en: They all fell to the earth in fear, and a voice spoke to him saying in Hebrew, "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" and made clear to him that his persecuting stance would not benefit him but would harm him, and likened his work to an ox kicking against iron goads (pricks).

26.11.0.en: Paul asked the speaker who He was, and He answered that He is Jesus whom he and his followers were persecuting.

26.12.0.en: Christ asked Paul to stand up and made clear to him that He had not appeared to him to punish him, but, as Ananias informed him afterward, that the Lord had chosen him to serve His name and witness to his faith, according to what he saw in the vision and what would appear to him afterward.

26.13.1.en: The Gentiles: this is an explanation before Agrippa, that he did not go to the Gentiles of himself but God sent him, and if this troubled the Jews it was because they hate the Gentiles.

26.13.2.en: Unto whom now I send thee: this confirms that Paul is an apostle from God.

26.13.3.en: God promised Paul that He would deliver him from the Jews and the Gentiles among whom he would serve, until he completed his ministry and at the end was martyred.

26.14.0.en: Paul declared that his preaching would open the eyes of those far off, that they might return to God from the darkness of sin and be freed from slavery to the devil and become children of God. And they would believe in the name of the Lord, and their sins would be forgiven them and they would receive a heavenly inheritance with the saints.

26.15.0.en: Paul determined to obey Christ who appeared to him in the vision, so he preached in His name in Damascus, where he was baptized, and in Jerusalem and all the region of Judea, and then to the Gentiles also, to call them to repentance and return to God and to live in righteousness in good works meet for repentance and the amendment of their conduct.

26.16.0.en: Because of Paul's preaching of the risen Christ and his preaching among the Gentiles without their needing to become Jews, the Jews seized him in the temple and wished to kill him.

26.17.0.en: The first that should rise from the dead: Christ was not the first to rise from the dead, for many had preceded Him in the Old Testament and He Himself had raised many, but He is the first who raised Himself and went to Paradise and the Kingdom, while the others went to Hades again because Christ had not yet accomplished redemption.

26.17.1.en: Paul made clear that God preserved him as He promised, as a witness to all of what Moses and the prophets foretold of the coming of Christ and His sufferings, as in Isaiah (ch. 53), and His resurrection, as in Hosea (Hos 6:2). Thus he proclaimed the light of the Gospel to the Jews and the Gentiles.

26.17.2.en: Paul always remembered Christ's call to him to serve Him. So do not forget the aim of your life, which is to live for God and prepare for your eternity, and to declare Christ by your love, and to call all to the pure life with God.

26.18.0.en: Festus was not convinced by Paul's words, so he interrupted him, crying out and accusing him that his much reading and study had made him lose his mind.

26.18.1.en: And this is always the opinion of Satan about the children of God, and he said it through the mouth of the Jews about Christ Himself (Jn 8:48), in order to hinder the preaching.

26.19.0.en: Most noble: a title of honor given to governors and persons of high station.

26.19.1.en: Paul answered Festus respectfully, saying that he was in full possession of his senses and mind, and was speaking the truth, which is God, so that the hearers might take heed and believe.

26.20.0.en: These things: the redemption of Christ and His resurrection and the preaching of Him.

26.20.1.en: This thing was not done in a corner: it did not happen in secret, away from sight.

26.20.2.en: Paul declared to Festus that King Agrippa knows, as a Jew, all these prophecies to which Paul pointed concerning the coming of Christ and His death and resurrection, and that he had heard of the preaching of Christ and His death and resurrection in Jerusalem, and indeed had also heard of the life of Christ and His crucifixion and resurrection, which was known to all the Jews.

26.21.0.en: Paul asked Agrippa whether he believed the words of the prophets, and Paul did not wait for the answer but answered for him, saying that he believes, in order to draw him to faith and to continue hearing the preaching of Christ.

26.22.0.en: Agrippa said that Paul wanted by this little, short talk to persuade him to Christianity, whereas the subject needs long study. By this he evaded answering, otherwise he would logically be forced in the end to declare his faith in Christ.

26.23.0.en: Paul said to Agrippa that he had prayed much to God for his faith and that of the hearers, whether by few or many words of preaching, but without their suffering the pains of bonds and imprisonment. This shows Paul's zeal to preach to every person and his tenderness toward everyone who hears him, that they should not meet persecutions and bonds after believing.

26.24.0.en: The council broke up and the king and the governor rose, and everyone followed them.

26.25.0.en: Those who had gathered in the assembly departed, convinced of Paul's innocence of what he was accused of.

26.26.0.en: Agrippa affirmed Paul's innocence, and that it would have been right to set him free at the hand of Felix or Festus, but because he had appealed to Caesar, it was necessary to send him to the capital, Rome.

26.26.1.en: The longing of every Christian is to draw others to the knowledge of Christ, whom he loved and became convinced of, as Paul did here, saying, "O taste and see that the Lord is good" (Ps 34:8), for the circumstances of the Christian's life never concern him more than the success of his witness and his mission.

26.26.2.en: The voyage from Caesarea to Malta
